en.title: Possessive adjectives
en.goal: Use mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses and the other possessive adjectives correctly.

blocks.title: My, our, your...
blocks.body: In French, the possessive adjective agrees with the gender and number of the thing owned — not with the owner! That is why "my" can be mon, ma or mes depending on the word that follows. (English does the opposite: his/her depends on the owner.)
examples: This is my brother. (frère is masculine)
This is my sister. (sœur is feminine)

blocks.title: Our, your (plural), their...
blocks.body: Notre/votre/leur (our, your (plural/formal), their), on the other hand, do not change with gender — they just get an "s" in the plural (nos/vos/leurs) whenever the thing owned is plural.

blocks.title: A sound-based exception
blocks.body: Before a feminine word that starts with a vowel (or a silent "h"), mon/ton/son are used instead of ma/ta/sa — just to avoid an awkward clash of two vowel sounds in a row. The word is still feminine; only the written form changes.
examples: This is my friend Sophie. (amie is feminine, but starts with a vowel)

review.pt: No francês, o adjetivo possessivo concorda com o gênero e número da coisa possuída — não com quem é o dono! ...
review.en: ... (English does the opposite: his/her depends on the owner.)
review.why: Added a one-sentence contrast with English (his/her follow the owner), which is true and helps English speakers; the original only compared to Portuguese.
Portuguese gender/number distinctions (meus/minhas) do not exist in English; glossed as "(plural)".

review.pt: seu / dele / dela; vosso / de vocês
review.why: English has no separate informal/formal "you" or Portuguese-style seu ambiguity; glosses adapted. Please check.
